sources.title: MySQL 8.4 InnoDB clustered and secondary indexes

claims.text: MySQL 8.4 CREATE TABLE syntax supports INDEX/KEY, PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FULLTEXT and SPATIAL definitions; KEY is synonymous with INDEX, an index may have multiple key parts, and index method support is storage-engine dependent.

MySQL 8.4 DDL documents PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE index definitions separately from nonunique INDEX/KEY definitions and duplicate unique-key detection. The candidate accurately treats this as a constraint/declaration dimension rather than a universal physical-index classification.

MySQL 8.4 documents column indexes and multiple-column indexes as separate query-design choices. The candidate deliberately avoids inventing a universal key-part order and requires concrete SQL, data distribution and EXPLAIN evidence for a specific ordering decision.

MySQL 8.4 documents FULLTEXT as a dedicated full-text index type and SPATIAL indexes as dedicated spatial indexes, including R-tree spatial indexes for supported InnoDB/MyISAM spatial columns. They are not synonyms for an ordinary B-tree declaration.
MySQL 8.4 documents that indexes help locate rows matching query conditions, while unnecessary indexes waste space and each additional index increases INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE maintenance cost.

MySQL 8.4 documents InnoDB clustered indexes storing row data and secondary index records carrying primary-key columns. It also documents that an index containing all columns required by a query can act as a covering index and may avoid reading table data. The candidate confines these statements to InnoDB and does not generalize them to every MySQL storage engine.

findings: The prior hard failure was evidence-scope debt rather than a false candidate statement: MySQL 8.4 primary documentation directly covers FULLTEXT, SPATIAL, multiple-column, constraint, InnoDB secondary/clustered and covering-index claims now mapped in the sidecar.

The candidate keeps classification dimensions separate, binds storage-engine-specific claims to InnoDB, and defers concrete composite-index ordering to actual SQL/data/EXPLAIN instead of presenting folklore as a universal rule.
